evidence.claim: Three prospectors found silver here in 1881, but extraction costs held investment down, and the town was almost deserted by 1890.

evidence.claim: A Montana Central Railway spur arrived the following year and made low-grade ore economical to ship to Great Falls.
evidence.quote: On November 15, 1891, a spur of the Montana Central Railway reached Neihart, and a strong mining boom began. Now even low-grade ore could be easily and cheaply shipped to the huge smelter in Great Falls.

flags: Visit Montana verifies the named 71-mile scenic byway and its recreational character, but the cache does not establish National Forest designation status or the catalog’s 1991 designation date. Omitted those formal designation claims.
The 1880s road toward White Sulphur Springs is regional road history, not proof that today’s U.S. 89 follows its exact alignment. Sources do not document construction of the present pass road.

Dropped the current assertion that 43 people live in Neihart now: cache 03 dates that population to the 2020 census. Dropped any implication that winter snow removal guarantees an open pass; the source says crews work to keep it open.

Sluice Boxes remains short because cache 07 has only a brief landscape description. Retained its exact title, coordinates and short walk kind, but no short, easy or currently open trail is verified by a site-manager source.

Observation tower existence is supported by cache 02; current tower access is not verified. Practical checked date records an offline review of Visit Montana’s winter warning. Showdown is background within the pass moment, not a separate business stop.
